newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Only three EU hopefuls up to scratch -document.
newsitem.headline: Only three EU hopefuls up to scratch -document.

text.p: Of 10 eastern European countries queueing for European Union membership, only three are up to scratch economically, a document prepared for the European Parliament said on Thursday.
"Economically Slovenia, the Czech Republic and Hungary are the main contenders for accession," the working paper drawn up for the EU assembly's budget committee said.
It said the three were the only ones to make the EU economic average in terms of purchasing power.
It said that in terms of purchasing power parity Slovenia achieved 55 percent of the average of the 15 EU member states in 1995. The Czech Republic achieved 51 percent and Hungary 42 per cent.

The data, released for a conference assessing the financial implications of the EU's drive to expand behind the former Iron Curtain, adds to pessimism setting in over the prospects for an early entry for any of the countries.
The data also adds to Poland's woes.

Originally seen as a frontrunner and one of the most urgent cases for EU membership, it has seen its record slipping in the home strait as the European Commission finalises assessments on how ready each candidate is to open early talks.
Although the data is unlikely to mean that Poland will be left out of the first enlargement wave, Poland only reached 29 percent of the EU average, the paper said.
"Poland's accession at the very beginning of eastward enlargement which several member states would like to see seems problematical in economic terms," it said.
"It will not be possible however for the decision on the accession of new member states to be taken without regard for political aspects," the paper said.
"It can therefore be assumed that Poland's accession in the first enlargement round would impose a considerable burden on the (EU) budget.

The paper said that if EU agricultural subsidy policies continued unchanged and the 10 joined at once, the EU's costs in the agricultural sector alone would rise by nine billion Ecus ($10.4 billion) in the year 2000.
The financial burden would mainly fall on the four existing EU members -- Spain, Portugal, Greece and Ireland -- who currently receive support to catch up with the richer ones, it said.
Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania are also in the queue for EU membership.
